data.text: The evidence is conclusive. The alert timestamps and the resolver's own log line up exactly, second-by-second.

data.cause: The primary resolver /opt/primary-dns/primary-dns on dns1.lan enforces a global ratelimit of only 20 q/s aggregated over the whole client subnet (ratelimit: 20 with ratelimit_subnet_len_ipv4: 24), so whenever the LAN briefly exceeds that burst it silently drops queries even for the locally-rewritten *.lan/nas.lan records, making clients' getaddrinfo return ENOTFOUND until the burst passes.
evidence: dns1.lan /opt/primary-dns/config.yaml sets 'ratelimit: 20' and 'ratelimit_subnet_len_ipv4: 24', alongside rewrites answering *.lan and nas.lan with 10.20.0.50 — i.e. the same low limit governs both recursion and local answers.

journalctl -u primary-dns on dns1.lan logs three bursts: 'ratelimit: 10.20.0.0/24 exceeded 20 q/s, dropping 23 queries' at Mar 03 02:14:00, 'dropping 31 queries' at 09:41:00 plus 'dropping 8 queries' at 09:41:30, and 'dropping 19 queries' at 13:02:00; each is immediately followed by a 'back under limit' line (02:14:01, 09:41:31, 13:02:01).

mon.lan journal shows the matching failures: '[media] WARN getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND media.lan' at 09:41:00, retry at 09:41:30, DOWN after 2 retries at 09:42:00, then UP (200) at 09:43:00; and '[nas] WARN getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND nas.lan' at 13:02:00 with '[nas] retry 1 ok (200)' at 13:02:30. The alert times coincide exactly with the ratelimit bursts on dns1.

dig @10.20.0.3 nas.lan from mon.lan returns 'nas.lan. 10 IN A 10.20.0.50' in 1 msec when no burst is active — the records exist and are correct, so the failures are dropped queries rather than missing data.

gw.lan /var/unbound/unbound.conf has a forward-zone for name "lan." pointing at forward-addr 10.20.0.3, and a query through that fallback (dig @10.20.0.1 nas.lan) came back NOERROR with ANSWER: 0 while the direct query to 10.20.0.3 answered — the backup resolver cannot serve local names independently.
Internet names are unaffected because gw.lan forwards '.' to DoH upstreams (1.1.1.2@853, 9.9.9.9@853 with forward-first: yes), which do not pass through dns1's rate limiter.
data.recommendation: Raise or exempt the rate limit on dns1.lan's primary-dns: increase ratelimit well above normal LAN burst (or set it to 0/disable it) and, more importantly, exclude the locally-answered .lan rewrite answers from rate limiting so internal lookups are never dropped. As a follow-up, make gw.lan able to answer local .lan names itself instead of only forwarding them to dns1, so the second DHCP-advertised resolver is a real fallback. Repeatedly restarting the service is not needed; this is a configuration threshold, not a crashed process.
data.detail: Aggressive per-subnet ratelimit on primary-dns drops legitimate LAN queries, including for local .lan records
